top_news.title: Brazil: Lula Should Focus on Human Rights in New Term
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image President-elect Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva voting in the second round of the 2022 presidential election, Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil. 2022 Rovena Rosa/Agncia Brasil (Sao Paulo, October 25, 2026) - Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has been reelected as Brazil's president, should use his new term to tackle chronic human rights problems, Human Rights Watch said today. President Lula defeated the Liberal Party candidate, Flavio Bolsonaro, in a runoff election on October 25, 2026, official results from the Superior Electoral Court show. Lula received 51.7 percent of the vote, while Bolsonaro received 48.2 percent, with 99.9 percent of the ballots counted, according to the Superior Electoral Court. "During his current term, President Lula has supported democratic institutions and made important progress on protecting forest and local communities who depend on it for their survival, but had a mixed record in other areas," saidCesar Munoz, Brazil director at Human Rights Watch. "His administration should address the record high numbers of killings by the police and other public security problems, and more consistently support human rights policies at home and abroad." News media reported reduced public transportation services in several states, which may have barred voters from reaching voting stations on October 25. Federal police were reportedly investigating possible electoral crimes. The Lula campaign asked for an extension in the voting time in some states due to those disruptions. The Bolsonaro campaign also asked for an extension in other areas of the country due to rain. As the polls were closing, a Supreme Court justice extended the voting time for two hours. Shortly after, the Electoral Court, and later the Supreme Court justice, established that the extension applied to voting stations that were still open. After taking office in January 2023, President Lula took important steps to repair some of thedamage that the previous administration had inflicted on democratic institutions, the environment, and human rights protections overall. Yet, chronic human rights problems continued to plague the country, including abuse by the police, which disproportionately affects Black Brazilians.Killings by police reached a record high-with 6,589 people killed in 2025-and had kept rising in 2026 as of September, driven by failed public policy strategies that have allowed the unchecked use of lethal force by police. Abusive police practices undermine public security-a primary concern for Brazilians, according tomany polls-by feeding mistrust and making communities less willing to collaborate with police, while fueling a cycle of violence that endangers both civilians and police officers. They also create an environment of impunity for excessive use of force in which police corruption and involvement with organized crime flourish. While public security is primarily the responsibility of states in Brazil, the federal government has a crucial role to play in coordinating and promoting public security policies that are more effective at dismantling criminal organizations, protecting the public from violence, and upholding human rights. An important measure to improve investigations that President Lula should support is to remove forensic services from police, to ensure independent analysis in police abuse cases and other crimes. During aninterview on October 15, President Lula defended trying and punishing as adults 16- and 17-year-old children accused of certain serious crimes. The measure wouldviolate international law, which says that children should be subject to justice systems that are distinct from those for adults. That proposal would also undermine rather than strengthen the country's efforts to reduce crime, Human Rights Watch said. Children who break the law can and should be held accountable, but in an individualized manner that promotes their rehabilitation. On the environment, President Lula should reverse inconsistencies that endanger the rights of Brazilians. His administration brought Amazon deforestation to thelowest level on record, according to official data, and resumed demarcating Indigenous territories. Yet, it took insufficient steps to regulate thecattle industry, historically the largest driver of deforestation and its related human rights abuses. His administration also initiated a long-awaited national program to reduce the use of pesticides. However, the administration continued to allow the use of highly hazardous pesticides, many of which are banned for use in the European Union and elsewhere because of proven harm to health and the environment. This puts Brazilians at risk ofacute poisoning and other serious health impacts, particularly Indigenous, Afro-descendant, and small farmers' communities. Major corruption scandals involving a range of politicians, political parties, and institutions have unfolded in recent years. The Lula administration should promote measures to strengthen the fight against corruption, including working with Congress to ensure transparency and oversight over budget allocations. Other long-standing human rights problems that President Lula should prioritize include gender-based violence, severe obstacles to abortion access, violence against human rights and environmental defenders, and the institutionalization of people with disabilities due to lack of sufficient community-based support services. Some incidents marred the electoral campaign. Non-profit organizations compiled134 cases of threats and violence against candidates and politicians from various parties, in the first 50 days of electoral campaign. Brazilian media alsoreported that Meta, which operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, restricted some content and features that promoted Lula's candidacy in the lead up to the election. Meta said it had experiencedtechnical issues but contended that it did not favor one candidate over another. Brazil's electoral courtordered Meta to take measures to ensure equal treatment of the candidates. Meta's Oversight Board-an external body that can overturn Meta's moderation decisions and provides non-binding policy guidance-expressed concern about recurrent failures in the company's "election integrity efforts," citing the "breakdown" that harmed Lula's campaign. "President Lula, who cannot run for office again in 2030, has a chance to leave a mark on the country by seeking solutions to long-standing problems that make a real difference in protecting rights and liberties for all Brazilians," Munoz said.

top_news.title: Captain Rahul Bali Honoured at 7th Odisha Tourism Conclave 2026 in Bhubaneswar
top_news.summary: Filmmaker, Indian Army Veteran and International Film Festival curator Captain Rahul Bali was honoured at the 7th Odisha Tourism Conclave 2026, held on 23 October in Bhubaneswar, in recognition of his work at the intersection of cinema, international cultural diplomacy and destination promotion. Organised by the Hotel & Restaurant Association of Odisha (HRAO), the mega event brought together more than 450 travel companies and tour operators from across India, alongside senior government representatives, tourism industry leaders, hospitality professionals, investors and other stakeholders committed to advancing Odisha's tourism potential. The prestigious conclave was attended by an eminent gathering of dignitaries and luminaries including His Excellency Dr. Braj Mohan Ram, Governor of Odisha; Smt. Pravati Parida, Deputy Chief Minister of Odisha; Smt. Anu Garg, Chief Secretary, Government of Odisha; Smt. Aparajita Sarangi, Member of Parliament; Shri Babu Singh, Member of the Legislative Assembly; and Dr. Madan Mohan Sethi, Consul General of India in Auckland, New Zealand. The event was hosted by HRAO under the leadership of Dr. J. K. Mohanty, Chairman of HRAO. The recognition of Captain Rahul Bali at this important tourism industry gathering underscores the growing relevance of cinema as a powerful medium for destination branding, international engagement and cultural exchange. With over three decades of experience in the Media and Entertainment industry, Captain Rahul Bali has built a distinctive professional journey spanning filmmaking, international film festival curation, cultural diplomacy and tourism promotion. A former Indian Army officer, Captain Bali is the Founder and Managing Director of Innovations India and is recognised for his efforts to use cinema as a bridge between nations, cultures and audiences. As an international film festival curator, he has curated Indian Film Festivals in Russia, Hungary, Poland, Kenya and Vietnam, creating platforms for Indian cinema to reach international audiences and strengthening cultural connections through the universal language of films. His work reflects a broader vision of positioning Indian cinema not merely as entertainment, but also as a strategic instrument for showcasing destinations, building international partnerships and encouraging people-to-people engagement. Captain Rahul Bali is the producer of the internationally awarded film Love in Vietnam and the upcoming Bollywood Film SILAA, and has been instrumental in laying the foundation for an India-Vietnam cinematic collaboration that brings together the creative worlds of Indian and Vietnamese cinema. These films exemplify how storytelling can transcend borders, showcase international destinations and create new avenues for cultural and tourism partnerships. Through these projects, Captain Bali is championing a model in which cinema, tourism and international partnerships work together to create lasting cultural and economic value. Such collaborations demonstrate how film productions can introduce international audiences to destinations, generate interest in travel and open new possibilities for tourism promotion. Odisha

top_news.title: 6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders - myMotherLode.com
top_news.summary: A new lawsuit against President Donald Trump's media ban stakes a claim for the public itself. The lawsuit was filed on behalf of six ordinary citizens. It argues that Trump's bans on media outlets whose content he dislikes violate the public's right to independent reporting about the government. Filed Monday in New York, the suit seeks not only restored media access for affected outlets, but broader relief on behalf of all journalists who cover the White House. The suit seeks to protect all news outlets from retaliation, now and in the future. The plaintiffs argue that restrictions on disfavored news organizations deprive the public of essential reporting.

top_news.title: Yemen: Houthi Attack on Taizz Road Threatens Lives, Welfare
top_news.summary: (Beirut) - The Houthi armed group on October 18, 2026, used explosives to severely damage a critical road into Yemen's besieged city of Taizz, putting civilian lives and welfare at increased risk, Human Rights Watch said today. The Hayjat al-Abd road has been the main entry point for food, medicine, and fuel to reach residents of Taizz city, which the Houthis havebesieged since 2015. Fighting in the area has primarily been between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government. The Houthis' deliberate destruction of segments of the road, if intended to disable infrastructure indispensable to civilian survival, would violate the laws of war and amount to a war crime. The attack may also have caused disproportionate civilian harm. "The Houthi attack on the remaining commercial supply route to besieged Taizz further endangers civilians already struggling with severe shortages of food, water, medicine, and fuel," said Niku Jafarnia, Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch. "If Taizz residents' access along this vital route is cut off for a prolonged period, they could face even greater risks to their lives and well-being." Human Rights Watch spoke to eight informed sources in October about two attacks on the road and their aftermath, including civil society workers and a relative of a witness to the October 18 attack. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery and verified photographs and a video from sources or posted on social media. In 2024, Human Rights Watch spoke with six Taizz residents about the difficulty of meeting basic needs during the Houthi siege. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Houthis on October 21 about attacks on the road but did not receive a response. Control over Taizz has been divided since 2015, when Houthi forces entered the governorate and surrounded its capital, Taizz city, Yemen's third largest city. The city has remained under Yemeni government control, but the Houthis have cut off vital roads connecting it to the rest of the country, notably the port city of Aden, the Yemeni government's current capital. While the laws of war do not prohibit sieges directed at military objectives, besieging forces are prohibited from using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare and must allow and facilitate humanitarian relief. Human Rights Watch has found that the Houthis'blocking of roads into Taizz has severely restricted civilians' ability to move in and out of the city and impeded the flow of essential goods,including water, and humanitarian access to the civilian population. Click to expand Image Graphic 2026 Human Rights Watch At about 4:00 a.m. on October 18, Houthi forces detonated explosives on the Hayjat al-Abd road in the town of al-Turba, significantly damaging a portion of the road. Residents in the area as well as two other informed sources said that the Houthis had been in control of al-Turba, about 75 kilometers south of Taizz city, since October 4. Since then, there had been no ground fighting in the area, including on the night of the attack. Nor had there been any indications that government forces or other armed groups were trying to re-enter the area, indicating that there was not another group that could have carried out the attack. Another source said his relative told him: "It was a massive and terrifying explosion-everyone woke up. Rocks reached all the way to my house." Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four photographs and a video from sources showing a damaged culvert on the switchbacks of the Hayjat al-Abd road. The damage is consistent with a subsurface detonation of explosives. Two weeks earlier, apparent Houthi forces had attacked the Hayjat al-Abd road about 85 kilometers southeast of Taizz city. A civil society worker in Taizz who spoke with several people knowledgeable about the attack said that on the night and early morning of September 30-October 1, Houthi forces and Yemeni government-aligned forces fought on several fronts around Taizz. The sources said that Houthi forces infiltrated and reached the Hayjat al-Abd road, placing and detonating explosives in a culvert under the road just past Souq al-Wahati, a local market. The Houthi forces then withdrew. Two other sources gave similar accounts based on communications with local residents. Human Rights Watch was unable to conclusively determine that Houthi forces carried out the attack. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated two additional photographs posted on social media on October 1 showing a damaged culvert on the Hayjat al-Abd road at the village of al-Muharraqah, where the road starts ascending to Taizz city. The damage to the culvert in the images is consistent with a subsurface detonation of explosives. Satellite imagery captured at 6:57 a.m. on October 1 shows damage to the culvert across the full width of the road. Government forces quickly retook the area after the first attack and later filled the destroyed portion of the road with dirt to allow vehicles to cross. Two sources said that government authorities had largely closed down the road to avoid further attacks on vehicles, though some vehicles continued to pass through. Since the October 1 attack, all roads into and out of Taizz have largely been blocked by Yemeni government-affiliated and Houthi forces due to hostilities. However, before the second attack, some supplies, including flour, had still been taken to Taizz city on the Hayjat al-Abd road, said two civil society workers in the area. However, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)said on October 14 that they had not been able to access the "more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance," which was "especially alarming" since most of Taizz's districts are considered to have emergency levels of hunger. The WFP also said that "wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted" in the city and that "remaining food supplies in local markets may last only a short time if access constraints continue." Under international humanitarian law, roads are presumptively civilian objects that become military objectives if by their nature, location, purpose, or use, they make an effective contribution to military action and their destruction, capture, or neutralization provides a definite military advantage at the time. Even if the Hayjat al-Abd road qualifies as a military objective, an attack would be unlawfully disproportionate if the expected incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Given the road's critical role in Taizz city civilians' access to food, water, medicine, and other basic needs, the assessment should account for the reasonably foreseeable consequences of damaging or closing it. The Houthis should have known, particularly given the UN'srepeatedwarnings, that supplies in Taizz were running out and that further closures after October 1 from attacks on the road could have grave effects for besieged Taizz civilians relying on the road for necessities. International humanitarian law also prohibits attacking, destroying, or rendering useless objects indispensable to the survival of a civilian population. The October 18 attack disrupted the remaining major commercial supply route to Taizz city. Whether it violated this prohibition depends on whether it was carried out for the purpose of denying civilians access to objects indispensable to their survival. Serious violations of the laws of war ordered or committed with criminal intent-that is, deliberately or recklessly-are war crimes. top_news.title: South Korea: Medication Abortion Rules Too Restrictive
top_news.summary: Click to expand Image A box of Mifepristone combined with Misoprostol tablets, May 2026. 2026 Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via AP Photo (Tokyo) - A South Korean government proposal would allow medication abortion in South Korea in 2027, but overly restrictive regulations will continue to impair the right of women and girls to safe and affordable abortion services, Human Rights Watch said today. National Assembly members have questioned government officials about the plan during a parliamentary audit. Seven years after South Korea's Constitutional Court ruled the country's decades-long abortion ban unconstitutional, effectively decriminalizing abortion and ordering legal reform by the end of 2020, the government has yet to amend the law to explicitly guarantee abortion rights. The government's new proposal would finally establish a regulatory framework for medication abortion using Mifegymiso, a combination of Misoprostol and Mifepristone recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the safest and most effective regimen. But access to the medication will remain unnecessarily impaired. "Allowing use of abortion pills is an important step, but South Korean lawmakers need to ensure that regulations aren't so restrictive that abortions are inaccessible and unaffordable," said Susanne Bergsten, acting women's rights research assistant at Human Rights Watch. "Access to safe abortion is essential to protecting the autonomy, health, and rights of women and girls." The draft rules would, for the first two years, permit medication abortions only up to nine weeks of pregnancy and specify that only doctors in large hospitals can prescribe and dispense the medication. If no side effects are found, it would likely be distributed more widely after the trial period. These restrictions are inconsistent with best practices, which endorse use of these medications up to 12 weeks, and with WHO recommendations that a broad range of health workers be authorized to manage medical abortion. Blocking many qualified providers from prescribing and dispensing the medication could hinder patients from receiving timely and critical care. Denying or delaying abortion access violates the rights to life, health, privacy, and freedom from discrimination. Mifepristone is approved by around 100 countries worldwide, and has been used safely in France and China for nearly 40 years. Major complications requiring hospitalization following medication abortion are very rare and occur in less than 1 percent of cases. The WHO also recommends telemedecine models of medical abortion care, in which prescriptions can be sent directly to pharmacies for self-administration at home. It considers this approach as safe for pregnancies of up to 12 weeks, provided the pregnant person has "accurate information, quality medicines and support from a trained health worker (if she needs or wants it during the process)." South Korea is obligated under international human rights law to ensure that all women and girls in the country can readily access timely, affordable, and safe abortion services. To meet these obligations, the National Assembly urgently needs to enact legislation that clarifies the decriminalization of abortion, and amends South Korea's Mother and Child Health Act to ensure that the rights of pregnant people are protected in all areas relevant to safe abortion care, including health care, counseling, and support services. Abortions should be available at a pregnant person's request, without requirements for parental or partner consent, notification or involvement, or accompaniment for adolescents or women with disabilities. Lawmakers should ensure that abortion services are covered by the National Health Insurance plan, to avoid costs becoming a barrier that prevents people from accessing abortion services. The government currently operates a crisis counseling system under the Special Act on Crisis Pregnancy and Protected Childbirth, enacted in 2023 for women and girls with unwanted or unintended pregnancies. However, the system has been criticized for not providing neutral advice and failing to provide adequate information about abortion, delaying access to abortion care. The law, which was intended to address unregistered births, also failed to introduce a comprehensive framework to ensure that all women in South Korea can register their child's birth, access pre- and postnatal care, receive financial support and services, and be free from the stigma and discrimination often faced by single mothers. The government should take genuine measures to support all pregnant people, whether they choose to continue or terminate a pregnancy by ensuring access to healthcare services throughout their pregnancy, at childbirth, and for childcare support. The government should also improve support and access to information for women and girls experiencing unintended or unwanted pregnancies. A 2023 report by Moimnet (Network to Assure Rights for Safe Abortion for All) found that many people face difficulties obtaining reliable abortion information. The government should provide unbiased information about reproductive health and abortion care, and ensure that schools deliver comprehensive, age-appropriate sexuality education. People seeking abortions should be able to make informed and autonomous decisions with support from healthcare providers who offer unbiased and respectful care. "South Korea's National Assembly should swiftly align abortion legislation with international human rights standards to protect patients and providers," Bergsten said. "Without safe and affordable access to abortion services, women and girls cannot fully experience their autonomy and reproductive rights."

articles.title: Brazil: Lula Should Focus on Human Rights in New Term
articles.summary: Click to expand Image President-elect Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva voting in the second round of the 2022 presidential election, Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil. 2022 Rovena Rosa/Agncia Brasil (Sao Paulo, October 25, 2026) - Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who has been reelected as Brazil's president, should use his new term to tackle chronic human rights problems, Human Rights Watch said today. President Lula defeated the Liberal Party candidate, Flavio Bolsonaro, in a runoff election on October 25, 2026, official results from the Superior Electoral Court show. Lula received 51.7 percent of the vote, while Bolsonaro received 48.2 percent, with 99.9 percent of the ballots counted, according to the Superior Electoral Court. "During his current term, President Lula has supported democratic institutions and made important progress on protecting forest and local communities who depend on it for their survival, but had a mixed record in other areas," saidCesar Munoz, Brazil director at Human Rights Watch. "His administration should address the record high numbers of killings by the police and other public security problems, and more consistently support human rights policies at home and abroad." News media reported reduced public transportation services in several states, which may have barred voters from reaching voting stations on October 25. Federal police were reportedly investigating possible electoral crimes. The Lula campaign asked for an extension in the voting time in some states due to those disruptions. The Bolsonaro campaign also asked for an extension in other areas of the country due to rain. As the polls were closing, a Supreme Court justice extended the voting time for two hours. Shortly after, the Electoral Court, and later the Supreme Court justice, established that the extension applied to voting stations that were still open. After taking office in January 2023, President Lula took important steps to repair some of thedamage that the previous administration had inflicted on democratic institutions, the environment, and human rights protections overall. Yet, chronic human rights problems continued to plague the country, including abuse by the police, which disproportionately affects Black Brazilians.Killings by police reached a record high-with 6,589 people killed in 2025-and had kept rising in 2026 as of September, driven by failed public policy strategies that have allowed the unchecked use of lethal force by police. Abusive police practices undermine public security-a primary concern for Brazilians, according tomany polls-by feeding mistrust and making communities less willing to collaborate with police, while fueling a cycle of violence that endangers both civilians and police officers. They also create an environment of impunity for excessive use of force in which police corruption and involvement with organized crime flourish. While public security is primarily the responsibility of states in Brazil, the federal government has a crucial role to play in coordinating and promoting public security policies that are more effective at dismantling criminal organizations, protecting the public from violence, and upholding human rights. An important measure to improve investigations that President Lula should support is to remove forensic services from police, to ensure independent analysis in police abuse cases and other crimes. During aninterview on October 15, President Lula defended trying and punishing as adults 16- and 17-year-old children accused of certain serious crimes. The measure wouldviolate international law, which says that children should be subject to justice systems that are distinct from those for adults. That proposal would also undermine rather than strengthen the country's efforts to reduce crime, Human Rights Watch said. Children who break the law can and should be held accountable, but in an individualized manner that promotes their rehabilitation. On the environment, President Lula should reverse inconsistencies that endanger the rights of Brazilians. His administration brought Amazon deforestation to thelowest level on record, according to official data, and resumed demarcating Indigenous territories. Yet, it took insufficient steps to regulate thecattle industry, historically the largest driver of deforestation and its related human rights abuses. His administration also initiated a long-awaited national program to reduce the use of pesticides. However, the administration continued to allow the use of highly hazardous pesticides, many of which are banned for use in the European Union and elsewhere because of proven harm to health and the environment. This puts Brazilians at risk ofacute poisoning and other serious health impacts, particularly Indigenous, Afro-descendant, and small farmers' communities. Major corruption scandals involving a range of politicians, political parties, and institutions have unfolded in recent years. The Lula administration should promote measures to strengthen the fight against corruption, including working with Congress to ensure transparency and oversight over budget allocations. Other long-standing human rights problems that President Lula should prioritize include gender-based violence, severe obstacles to abortion access, violence against human rights and environmental defenders, and the institutionalization of people with disabilities due to lack of sufficient community-based support services. Some incidents marred the electoral campaign. Non-profit organizations compiled134 cases of threats and violence against candidates and politicians from various parties, in the first 50 days of electoral campaign. Brazilian media alsoreported that Meta, which operates Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, restricted some content and features that promoted Lula's candidacy in the lead up to the election. Meta said it had experiencedtechnical issues but contended that it did not favor one candidate over another. Brazil's electoral courtordered Meta to take measures to ensure equal treatment of the candidates. Meta's Oversight Board-an external body that can overturn Meta's moderation decisions and provides non-binding policy guidance-expressed concern about recurrent failures in the company's "election integrity efforts," citing the "breakdown" that harmed Lula's campaign. "President Lula, who cannot run for office again in 2030, has a chance to leave a mark on the country by seeking solutions to long-standing problems that make a real difference in protecting rights and liberties for all Brazilians," Munoz said.

articles.title: Captain Rahul Bali Honoured at 7th Odisha Tourism Conclave 2026 in Bhubaneswar
articles.summary: Filmmaker, Indian Army Veteran and International Film Festival curator Captain Rahul Bali was honoured at the 7th Odisha Tourism Conclave 2026, held on 23 October in Bhubaneswar, in recognition of his work at the intersection of cinema, international cultural diplomacy and destination promotion. Organised by the Hotel & Restaurant Association of Odisha (HRAO), the mega event brought together more than 450 travel companies and tour operators from across India, alongside senior government representatives, tourism industry leaders, hospitality professionals, investors and other stakeholders committed to advancing Odisha's tourism potential. The prestigious conclave was attended by an eminent gathering of dignitaries and luminaries including His Excellency Dr. Braj Mohan Ram, Governor of Odisha; Smt. Pravati Parida, Deputy Chief Minister of Odisha; Smt. Anu Garg, Chief Secretary, Government of Odisha; Smt. Aparajita Sarangi, Member of Parliament; Shri Babu Singh, Member of the Legislative Assembly; and Dr. Madan Mohan Sethi, Consul General of India in Auckland, New Zealand. The event was hosted by HRAO under the leadership of Dr. J. K. Mohanty, Chairman of HRAO. The recognition of Captain Rahul Bali at this important tourism industry gathering underscores the growing relevance of cinema as a powerful medium for destination branding, international engagement and cultural exchange. With over three decades of experience in the Media and Entertainment industry, Captain Rahul Bali has built a distinctive professional journey spanning filmmaking, international film festival curation, cultural diplomacy and tourism promotion. A former Indian Army officer, Captain Bali is the Founder and Managing Director of Innovations India and is recognised for his efforts to use cinema as a bridge between nations, cultures and audiences. As an international film festival curator, he has curated Indian Film Festivals in Russia, Hungary, Poland, Kenya and Vietnam, creating platforms for Indian cinema to reach international audiences and strengthening cultural connections through the universal language of films. His work reflects a broader vision of positioning Indian cinema not merely as entertainment, but also as a strategic instrument for showcasing destinations, building international partnerships and encouraging people-to-people engagement. Captain Rahul Bali is the producer of the internationally awarded film Love in Vietnam and the upcoming Bollywood Film SILAA, and has been instrumental in laying the foundation for an India-Vietnam cinematic collaboration that brings together the creative worlds of Indian and Vietnamese cinema. These films exemplify how storytelling can transcend borders, showcase international destinations and create new avenues for cultural and tourism partnerships. Through these projects, Captain Bali is championing a model in which cinema, tourism and international partnerships work together to create lasting cultural and economic value. Such collaborations demonstrate how film productions can introduce international audiences to destinations, generate interest in travel and open new possibilities for tourism promotion. Odisha

articles.title: 6 citizens sue Trump, saying media ban deprives them of news as audience stakeholders - myMotherLode.com
articles.summary: A new lawsuit against President Donald Trump's media ban stakes a claim for the public itself. The lawsuit was filed on behalf of six ordinary citizens. It argues that Trump's bans on media outlets whose content he dislikes violate the public's right to independent reporting about the government. Filed Monday in New York, the suit seeks not only restored media access for affected outlets, but broader relief on behalf of all journalists who cover the White House. The suit seeks to protect all news outlets from retaliation, now and in the future. The plaintiffs argue that restrictions on disfavored news organizations deprive the public of essential reporting.

articles.title: Yemen: Houthi Attack on Taizz Road Threatens Lives, Welfare
articles.summary: (Beirut) - The Houthi armed group on October 18, 2026, used explosives to severely damage a critical road into Yemen's besieged city of Taizz, putting civilian lives and welfare at increased risk, Human Rights Watch said today. The Hayjat al-Abd road has been the main entry point for food, medicine, and fuel to reach residents of Taizz city, which the Houthis havebesieged since 2015. Fighting in the area has primarily been between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government. The Houthis' deliberate destruction of segments of the road, if intended to disable infrastructure indispensable to civilian survival, would violate the laws of war and amount to a war crime. The attack may also have caused disproportionate civilian harm. "The Houthi attack on the remaining commercial supply route to besieged Taizz further endangers civilians already struggling with severe shortages of food, water, medicine, and fuel," said Niku Jafarnia, Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch. "If Taizz residents' access along this vital route is cut off for a prolonged period, they could face even greater risks to their lives and well-being." Human Rights Watch spoke to eight informed sources in October about two attacks on the road and their aftermath, including civil society workers and a relative of a witness to the October 18 attack. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery and verified photographs and a video from sources or posted on social media. In 2024, Human Rights Watch spoke with six Taizz residents about the difficulty of meeting basic needs during the Houthi siege. Human Rights Watch wrote to the Houthis on October 21 about attacks on the road but did not receive a response. Control over Taizz has been divided since 2015, when Houthi forces entered the governorate and surrounded its capital, Taizz city, Yemen's third largest city. The city has remained under Yemeni government control, but the Houthis have cut off vital roads connecting it to the rest of the country, notably the port city of Aden, the Yemeni government's current capital. While the laws of war do not prohibit sieges directed at military objectives, besieging forces are prohibited from using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare and must allow and facilitate humanitarian relief. Human Rights Watch has found that the Houthis'blocking of roads into Taizz has severely restricted civilians' ability to move in and out of the city and impeded the flow of essential goods,including water, and humanitarian access to the civilian population. Click to expand Image Graphic 2026 Human Rights Watch At about 4:00 a.m. on October 18, Houthi forces detonated explosives on the Hayjat al-Abd road in the town of al-Turba, significantly damaging a portion of the road. Residents in the area as well as two other informed sources said that the Houthis had been in control of al-Turba, about 75 kilometers south of Taizz city, since October 4. Since then, there had been no ground fighting in the area, including on the night of the attack. Nor had there been any indications that government forces or other armed groups were trying to re-enter the area, indicating that there was not another group that could have carried out the attack. Another source said his relative told him: "It was a massive and terrifying explosion-everyone woke up. Rocks reached all the way to my house." Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated four photographs and a video from sources showing a damaged culvert on the switchbacks of the Hayjat al-Abd road. The damage is consistent with a subsurface detonation of explosives. Two weeks earlier, apparent Houthi forces had attacked the Hayjat al-Abd road about 85 kilometers southeast of Taizz city. A civil society worker in Taizz who spoke with several people knowledgeable about the attack said that on the night and early morning of September 30-October 1, Houthi forces and Yemeni government-aligned forces fought on several fronts around Taizz. The sources said that Houthi forces infiltrated and reached the Hayjat al-Abd road, placing and detonating explosives in a culvert under the road just past Souq al-Wahati, a local market. The Houthi forces then withdrew. Two other sources gave similar accounts based on communications with local residents. Human Rights Watch was unable to conclusively determine that Houthi forces carried out the attack. Human Rights Watch verified and geolocated two additional photographs posted on social media on October 1 showing a damaged culvert on the Hayjat al-Abd road at the village of al-Muharraqah, where the road starts ascending to Taizz city. The damage to the culvert in the images is consistent with a subsurface detonation of explosives. Satellite imagery captured at 6:57 a.m. on October 1 shows damage to the culvert across the full width of the road. Government forces quickly retook the area after the first attack and later filled the destroyed portion of the road with dirt to allow vehicles to cross. Two sources said that government authorities had largely closed down the road to avoid further attacks on vehicles, though some vehicles continued to pass through. Since the October 1 attack, all roads into and out of Taizz have largely been blocked by Yemeni government-affiliated and Houthi forces due to hostilities. However, before the second attack, some supplies, including flour, had still been taken to Taizz city on the Hayjat al-Abd road, said two civil society workers in the area. However, the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP)said on October 14 that they had not been able to access the "more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance," which was "especially alarming" since most of Taizz's districts are considered to have emergency levels of hunger. The WFP also said that "wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted" in the city and that "remaining food supplies in local markets may last only a short time if access constraints continue." Under international humanitarian law, roads are presumptively civilian objects that become military objectives if by their nature, location, purpose, or use, they make an effective contribution to military action and their destruction, capture, or neutralization provides a definite military advantage at the time. Even if the Hayjat al-Abd road qualifies as a military objective, an attack would be unlawfully disproportionate if the expected incidental civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated. Given the road's critical role in Taizz city civilians' access to food, water, medicine, and other basic needs, the assessment should account for the reasonably foreseeable consequences of damaging or closing it. The Houthis should have known, particularly given the UN'srepeatedwarnings, that supplies in Taizz were running out and that further closures after October 1 from attacks on the road could have grave effects for besieged Taizz civilians relying on the road for necessities. International humanitarian law also prohibits attacking, destroying, or rendering useless objects indispensable to the survival of a civilian population. The October 18 attack disrupted the remaining major commercial supply route to Taizz city. articles.title: South Korea: Medication Abortion Rules Too Restrictive
articles.summary: Click to expand Image A box of Mifepristone combined with Misoprostol tablets, May 2026. 2026 Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via AP Photo (Tokyo) - A South Korean government proposal would allow medication abortion in South Korea in 2027, but overly restrictive regulations will continue to impair the right of women and girls to safe and affordable abortion services, Human Rights Watch said today. National Assembly members have questioned government officials about the plan during a parliamentary audit. Seven years after South Korea's Constitutional Court ruled the country's decades-long abortion ban unconstitutional, effectively decriminalizing abortion and ordering legal reform by the end of 2020, the government has yet to amend the law to explicitly guarantee abortion rights. The government's new proposal would finally establish a regulatory framework for medication abortion using Mifegymiso, a combination of Misoprostol and Mifepristone recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the safest and most effective regimen. But access to the medication will remain unnecessarily impaired. "Allowing use of abortion pills is an important step, but South Korean lawmakers need to ensure that regulations aren't so restrictive that abortions are inaccessible and unaffordable," said Susanne Bergsten, acting women's rights research assistant at Human Rights Watch. "Access to safe abortion is essential to protecting the autonomy, health, and rights of women and girls." The draft rules would, for the first two years, permit medication abortions only up to nine weeks of pregnancy and specify that only doctors in large hospitals can prescribe and dispense the medication. If no side effects are found, it would likely be distributed more widely after the trial period. These restrictions are inconsistent with best practices, which endorse use of these medications up to 12 weeks, and with WHO recommendations that a broad range of health workers be authorized to manage medical abortion. Blocking many qualified providers from prescribing and dispensing the medication could hinder patients from receiving timely and critical care. Denying or delaying abortion access violates the rights to life, health, privacy, and freedom from discrimination. Mifepristone is approved by around 100 countries worldwide, and has been used safely in France and China for nearly 40 years. Major complications requiring hospitalization following medication abortion are very rare and occur in less than 1 percent of cases. The WHO also recommends telemedecine models of medical abortion care, in which prescriptions can be sent directly to pharmacies for self-administration at home. It considers this approach as safe for pregnancies of up to 12 weeks, provided the pregnant person has "accurate information, quality medicines and support from a trained health worker (if she needs or wants it during the process)." South Korea is obligated under international human rights law to ensure that all women and girls in the country can readily access timely, affordable, and safe abortion services. To meet these obligations, the National Assembly urgently needs to enact legislation that clarifies the decriminalization of abortion, and amends South Korea's Mother and Child Health Act to ensure that the rights of pregnant people are protected in all areas relevant to safe abortion care, including health care, counseling, and support services. Abortions should be available at a pregnant person's request, without requirements for parental or partner consent, notification or involvement, or accompaniment for adolescents or women with disabilities. Lawmakers should ensure that abortion services are covered by the National Health Insurance plan, to avoid costs becoming a barrier that prevents people from accessing abortion services. The government currently operates a crisis counseling system under the Special Act on Crisis Pregnancy and Protected Childbirth, enacted in 2023 for women and girls with unwanted or unintended pregnancies. However, the system has been criticized for not providing neutral advice and failing to provide adequate information about abortion, delaying access to abortion care. The law, which was intended to address unregistered births, also failed to introduce a comprehensive framework to ensure that all women in South Korea can register their child's birth, access pre- and postnatal care, receive financial support and services, and be free from the stigma and discrimination often faced by single mothers. The government should take genuine measures to support all pregnant people, whether they choose to continue or terminate a pregnancy by ensuring access to healthcare services throughout their pregnancy, at childbirth, and for childcare support. The government should also improve support and access to information for women and girls experiencing unintended or unwanted pregnancies. A 2023 report by Moimnet (Network to Assure Rights for Safe Abortion for All) found that many people face difficulties obtaining reliable abortion information. The government should provide unbiased information about reproductive health and abortion care, and ensure that schools deliver comprehensive, age-appropriate sexuality education. People seeking abortions should be able to make informed and autonomous decisions with support from healthcare providers who offer unbiased and respectful care. "South Korea's National Assembly should swiftly align abortion legislation with international human rights standards to protect patients and providers," Bergsten said. "Without safe and affordable access to abortion services, women and girls cannot fully experience their autonomy and reproductive rights."
